To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the effect of the nutrition on bowel symptoms from RT was inconclusive, although minor and transient improvements in some symptoms were observed.
the effects of a dietary intervention on bowel symptoms from radiotherapy for prostate cancer were small and inconclusive.
the nutrition intervention had no effect on bowel symptoms or health-related quality of the life.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of nutrition on health-related quality of live in patients with cancer.
the impact of nutrition on bowel symptoms and quality of life in men with prostate cancer who have undergone radiotherapy to the pelvic region.
the effects of a dietary intervention aiming at reducing the adverse effects of radiotherapy to the prostate and pelvis, and the effects on health-related quality oflife.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the intervention was ineffective.
there is no evidence to support or refute the use of dietary fibre and lactos reduction as a nutrition intervention to reduce bowel symptoms from pelvic radiotherapy.
there is no evidence to support or refute the hypothesis that a dietary intervention of this nature would reduce adverse effects in patients with prostate receiving pelvic radiotherapy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a nutrition intervention aiming to replace insoluable fibres with soluble, and reduce intake of dairy products, had a small effect on bowel symptoms in patients with prostate carcinoma undergoing pelvic radiotherapy.

a nutrition intervention aiming at replacing insoluble fibre with soluble and reduce lactose intake did not improve bowel symptoms or health-related quality of the life in patients with prostate carcinoma treated with pelvic radiotherapy, compared with standard advice.
the nutrition intervention was not effective in reducing the acute and late bowel side effects of radiotherapy in patients who received radiotherapy for prostate cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a nutrition intervention with the aim of reducing fibre intake and lactose consumption does not reduce the adverse effects of radiotherapy to the prostate.
the nutrition intervention was not associated with clinically important changes in bowel symptoms or quality of life.

a nutrition intervention aiming to replace insolube fibre with soluble and reduce lactose intake does not reduce bowel symptoms and improve health-related quality oflife in patients treated with pelvic radiotherapy for prostate cancer.
